heading: Side chair, Gothic Revival style; probably American, about 1840–50; maker unknown; reddish-brown wood (probably mahogany or rosewood), silk damask upholstery, brass casters
paragraph: The chair's design draws on the architecture of medieval churches. The tall back is shaped as a pointed arch and edged with carved crockets, and a carved finial sits at the top. On either side, the back posts rise as ringed shafts that taper to points like small spires. Gothic Revival furniture of this kind was made for halls and libraries in the 1840s, when architects and furniture makers took up medieval forms. The red upholstery has a lattice of diamonds and foliate medallions. From the photograph alone it is not possible to tell whether the upholstery is original or a later replacement. The turned front legs run on brass casters.

heading: Cylinder seal and modern impression; probably northern Mesopotamia or Syria, probably mid-2nd millennium BCE; dark stone
paragraph: A cylinder seal was rolled across damp clay to mark ownership or seal a document or container. The design is cut into the seal in reverse, so it reads correctly only on the impression. The modern impression shown here lets the whole scene be seen at once. Horned animals, probably goats, stand among stylized trees, and some of them turn their heads back. A bird flies above, small star or rosette shapes fill the gaps, and a tall serpent rises at one end. Two lines run along the top and bottom as borders. The style suggests a seal from the Syro-Mesopotamian region in the second millennium BCE. The stone has not been identified.

heading: Spearhead; probably European, probably 16th–17th century; maker unknown; steel, wood
paragraph: The spearhead has a long, narrow blade that tapers to a sharp point. Partway down, the blade narrows in a small step on one edge. Below the blade, a faceted socket fits over a wooden shaft and is fixed to it with a pin or rivet. A head this slender was made to pierce armour or padding rather than to cut. The surface is bright, with scattered small pits. The photograph shows only the head and the top of the shaft, and it gives no scale, so the weapon's full length cannot be stated here. No maker's mark is visible.

heading: Pin with bird finial; probably Andean, Peru, before 1532; maker unknown; copper or copper alloy
paragraph: At the top of this long, tapering pin is a bird with a crest and a raised tail, standing on a small platform. Just below the head, a hole runs through the shaft, perhaps for a cord or chain. In the Andes, long metal pins held garments closed, and pins with figures on their heads were made as well as plain ones. The metal is dark, with a worn, uneven surface. Specks of red near the point may be pigment or corrosion; the photograph does not settle which. Where it was found, and its exact date, are not known from the photograph.

heading: Travelers Above Yokohama Harbor, Seen through a Hillside Cutting. Japan, Edo period, about 1860. Gountei (Utagawa) Sadahide (1807–1878/79). Woodblock print; ink and color on paper.
paragraph: Framed by the steep walls of a cutting and by leaning pines, a small party of travelers pauses above a wide bay. Two men walk ahead. One wears a green jacket with a white crest and the other carries a bundle on his back. Two women follow below, and a fan lies at the lower left. Square-rigged foreign ships crowd the harbor. The scene is almost certainly Yokohama, opened to foreign trade in 1859, which Sadahide pictured many times for buyers eager to see the new port. The signature at lower right reads Gountei Sadahide. The photograph is too small to read the full inscription in the red cartouche at the top.

heading: Cavalryman Standing beside His Horse. France, dated 1872 (reading uncertain). Édouard Detaille (1848–1912). Watercolor and gouache on tan paper.
paragraph: A heavy-cavalry guardsman in full dress stands at ease. His gloved hand rests on his sword hilt and his black horse waits behind him. Detaille, whose signature is at lower left, built his reputation on painting the French army with near-documentary exactness. The steel helmet with red plume and horsehair mane, blue sleeves, gold aiguillettes, red sash and tall boots appear to be the uniform of the Cent-gardes, Napoleon III's mounted bodyguard, which was disbanded in 1870. If the date beside the signature reads 1872, this is a remembrance of a vanished corps. The bare brown ground, with only a cast shadow, keeps attention on the uniform.

heading: Shabti. Egypt, probably Third Intermediate Period (about 1070–664 B.C.). Faience.
paragraph: Shabtis were placed in Egyptian tombs to do, in the deceased's place, any labor demanded of them in the afterlife. This small figure has the mummiform shape: a wrapped body with feet set on a low base, arms crossed on the chest, and a long wig falling over the shoulders. Its bright turquoise glaze, typical of Egyptian faience, has worn through in pale patches. Dark traces near the hands may be what remains of painted details such as hoes. No inscription is visible in this view, so the date rests on style alone. Figures like this were made in large numbers, sometimes hundreds for a single burial.

heading: Medal of Edward I, from a Series of the Kings of England. Probably Geneva, about 1731. Jean Dassier (Swiss, 1676–1763). Bronze.
paragraph: The legend around this crowned bust reads, in part, EDOUARD I D G ANG ET HIB REX, which means "Edward I, by the grace of God, King of England and Ireland." The portrait is not a true likeness. Edward died in 1307, and this idealized face, with long curled hair, a jeweled crown and a mantle fastened with a jeweled clasp, is an eighteenth-century invention. The medal appears to come from the series of English monarchs issued by the Geneva medalist Jean Dassier around 1731 and sold as sets to collectors. Only the obverse is shown here. In that series the reverse carries a historical inscription.

heading: Fragment of a red-figure vase, probably Attic, probably 5th century BC; terracotta with black gloss
paragraph: This small sherd, about 2 cm long, was broken from the wall of a painted Greek pot. The clay was left its natural orange, and the dark areas were painted in a glossy black slip that fired black. The reserved tongue-shaped areas set against the black are typical of the red-figure technique. Such a small piece cannot tell us what the scene showed: the marks could belong to hair, drapery, or a floral ornament. The painter and the vessel's shape are unknown. Fragments like this are kept in study collections, where they record painting technique and help scholars match pieces from the same workshops. The inventory number 2011.604.1.2486 is written on the card beside it.

heading: Star-shaped tile, Iran or Central Asia, probably Timurid period, 15th century; glazed earthenware, polychrome glaze
paragraph: This tile was made to fit with others into a wall revetment. Star tiles like this one were usually set with cross-shaped tiles in a continuous field. Its star outline is decorated with a pattern of six-fold symmetry. White strapwork forms pointed lobed medallions on a deep cobalt-blue ground, and in each one sits a red-and-yellow blossom around a central rosette. A turquoise band follows the edge. The colours are separated by thin dark lines, which suggests the cuerda seca technique. This method let several glazes be fired on one tile without running together. The glaze is finely crazed, and the chipped edges show a reddish body underneath.

heading: Fragment of a glass object, perhaps a vessel base; place and date of manufacture undetermined; dark glass with applied opaque white trail
paragraph: This broken piece of glass looks black in reflected light. An opaque white glass trail was applied around it as a raised ring while the glass was still hot. Inside the ring, the dark glass forms a domed, pushed-in centre, much like the kick of a small bottle or flask base. The piece may instead come from another object, such as a large bead. Soil is still caught in its hollows, which suggests it came from the ground. No scale is included in the photograph, and nothing visible shows where or when it was made. Contrasting trails of this kind were used by glassworkers over many centuries.

heading: Rattle; maker, place and date unknown; gourd (?), bone, plant fibre
paragraph: The egg-shaped brown head of this rattle seems to be a dried gourd or another hard shell. Shaken, the seeds or pebbles inside would have rattled against its walls. A row of small holes was pierced around the opening at the narrow end. Cords of plant fibre run through these holes to bind the head tightly to a handle. The handle looks like a long bone with its joint still at the end, possibly from a bird or small animal. The materials suggest a rattle made for music, dance or ceremony. The photograph does not show where it was made, who used it, or what it contains. A small red mark on the shell may be an old collection number.

heading: Side chair, Gothic Revival style. United States, ca. 1845–55. Maker unidentified. Probably rosewood or mahogany, with silk damask upholstery and brass casters.
paragraph: The chair applies the architecture of a Gothic church to a piece of furniture. Its tall upholstered back rises to a pointed arch. The arch carries carved crockets and ends in a fleur-de-lis finial. Ring-turned posts, cut like stalks of bamboo, stand at either side and end in slender pinnacles. Furniture like this was made for the Gothic villas and libraries that American architects designed in the 1840s, and it was meant to look picturesque more than to be practical. The red damask, a pattern of lozenges and medallions, is probably a later replacement and not the original cover. The caster wheels let the heavy chair be moved across the room.

heading: View of Yokohama Harbor from a Cutting in the Hills. Japan, Edo period, ca. 1860. Utagawa (Gountei) Sadahide (1807–1879). Woodblock print (nishiki-e); ink and color on paper.
paragraph: Travelers climb a steep path cut through a hill. Two men walk ahead, and behind them come women and children. Between the cliff walls, which are framed by pines, the land opens onto a harbor full of ships, with a settlement laid out in grid-like rows along the shore. Yokohama was opened to foreign trade in 1859, and Sadahide was one of the most prolific artists to record the new port. Prints like this one sold to people curious about the foreigners and their ships. A red cartouche at the top holds a descriptive inscription, which has not been fully transcribed here. The red cartouche at lower right holds the artist's signature, and seals sit beside it.

heading: Cylinder seal with animals, serpent and tree, and modern impression. Probably northern Mesopotamia or Syria, Mitanni period, ca. 1500–1300 B.C. Carver unknown. Dark stone, possibly serpentine.
paragraph: A cylinder seal was rolled across wet clay to mark ownership or to authenticate tablets, jar sealings and door sealings. It was usually pierced lengthwise so that it could be worn on a cord. The modern impression beside it shows the full design. Horned animals, probably goats or gazelles, stand in a row. Among them are a rearing serpent, a long-necked bird, a branching tree and small star-shaped motifs. A plain band runs along the top and bottom. The animals are cut with simple drilled and linear strokes, and that carving is typical of the "common style" seals of the period. No scale was photographed, so the seal's size is not given here.

heading: Cavalryman in Full Dress Standing beside His Horse. France, late 19th century. Édouard Detaille (French, 1848–1912). Watercolor and gouache on toned paper
paragraph: A mounted soldier has dismounted and stands at ease beside a dark horse, one gloved hand resting on his sword. He wears a crested brass helmet with a red plume, a blue coat with red facings and a red sash, white breeches and tall jackboots. Detaille was France's leading painter of military life and uniform, and he made many careful studies like this one. The plain brown ground has no setting, so the eye goes straight to the accoutrements, which are painted in exact detail. The sheet is signed lower left. The regiment and the period of the uniform are not identified here.

heading: Star-Shaped Tile. Central Asia or Iran, probably 15th century (Timurid period). Stonepaste, polychrome glazes in cuerda seca technique
paragraph: This ten-pointed star is edged in turquoise and filled with cobalt blue. A white strapwork rosette is laid over the blue, with turquoise stems, red-brown and yellow blossoms, and small white buds in the points. Each colour sits in its own field, kept apart by thin, slightly recessed lines. This is the cuerda seca ("dry cord") technique, which let potters fire several glaze colours on one tile without them running together. A tile like this would have been set with others in a wall revetment of a Timurid mosque, shrine or palace. The glaze is finely crazed and the edges are chipped.

paragraph: This long, slender steel head narrows to a needle point. About a third of the way up from the base the blade steps in sharply, and above that point it continues as a narrower, stiffer section built to thrust and to pierce. Below the blade a faceted socket fits over a wooden shaft, part of which survives. Heads of this form were mounted on infantry spears and pikes, which could reach well beyond a sword's length. The place and date given here are an estimate from the form of the head.

heading: Shabti. Egypt, probably Third Intermediate Period (ca. 1070–664 B.C.). Faience
paragraph: This small figure is mummiform. Its arms are crossed over the chest and it wears a long tripartite wig. A bright turquoise-blue glaze covers it, now spotted with dark patches where the glaze has worn or discoloured. Shabtis were placed in tombs in great numbers to stand in for the dead person when the gods called on them to work in the fields of the afterlife. The figure probably held farming tools in its hands, but these have worn away. No inscription can be read in this view. The bright blue glaze and simple modelling suggest a date in the Third Intermediate Period.

paragraph: Edward I, who ruled England from 1272 to 1307, is shown in profile bust, crowned and draped. His wavy hair falls to his shoulders, and a beaded chain clasps the cloak across his chest. The legend reads EDOUARD·I·D·G·ANG·ET·HIB·REX, which means "Edward I, by the grace of God, King of England and Ireland." The French spelling of the name points to the medal's Genevan maker. Around 1731, Jean Dassier produced a retrospective series of English monarchs for collectors, and this portrait is imagined rather than taken from life. In this series the reverse usually carries a Latin summary of the reign. It is not shown here.

heading: Rattle. Place, date and maker not known. Gourd, bone (?), plant-fibre cord
paragraph: A hollow, egg-shaped gourd forms the sound chamber of this rattle. Seeds or pebbles inside would sound when it was shaken, though the photograph cannot show what it holds. The handle appears to be an animal long bone, with its knobbed joint end left at the base. The bone fits into the gourd's narrow end. It is lashed in place with fibre cord threaded through a ring of small holes pierced around the opening. A small red mark near the gourd's lower edge may be a collection number. Gourd rattles have been made in many parts of the world, and nothing in this view identifies where this one comes from.

heading: Side chair, Gothic Revival style; United States, 1850–60; maker unknown; wood, with silk damask upholstery and brass casters
paragraph: The chair's design draws on the architecture of medieval churches. The tall back is shaped as a pointed arch and edged with carved crockets, and a carved finial sits at the top. On either side, the back posts rise as ringed shafts that taper to spire-like points. In the mid-nineteenth century, American furniture makers and their clients used medieval forms like these for halls and libraries. The red upholstery has a lattice of diamonds and foliate medallions. The museum's record does not describe the upholstery, so it may be original or a later replacement. The turned front legs run on brass casters. The chair stands about 126 cm (49¾ in.) high.

heading: Cylinder seal and modern impression; Cyprus, Late Cypriot period, about 15th–13th century BCE; steatite
paragraph: A cylinder seal was rolled across damp clay to mark ownership or seal a document or container. The design is cut into the seal in reverse, so it reads correctly only on the impression. The modern impression shows the whole scene at once. Horned animals, probably goats, stand among stylized trees, and some turn their heads back. A bird flies above, small star or rosette shapes fill the gaps, and a tall serpent rises at one end. Cypriot seal cutters of this period borrowed motifs like these from the seals of Syria and northern Mesopotamia. The seal is 3.25 cm (1¼ in.) high. It came from the Cesnola Collection.

heading: Couteau de brèche (staff weapon); France, about 1500; maker unknown; steel, beech wood
paragraph: The French name means "breach knife". The couteau de brèche is a staff weapon: a long, knife-like blade set on a wooden shaft. This one is almost two metres long, and the head alone is 61 cm. Seen here from an angle, the blade looks like a slender spear point. Partway down it narrows in a step on one edge, and below the blade a faceted socket is pinned to the beech shaft. The photograph shows only the head and the top of the shaft. The bright steel has scattered small pits, and no maker's mark is visible. The weapon weighs about 2 kg.

heading: Pin (catalogued as a knife) with animal finial; Moche, Peru, 2nd–7th century; maker unknown; cast copper
paragraph: At the top of this cast copper implement is a crested animal standing on a small platform. Its crest and raised tail suggest a bird. The museum's record gives two different names for the object: its title calls it a pin, and its object name calls it a knife. In the photograph the shaft is rounded and tapers to a point, and no cutting edge is visible, so it is shown here as a pin. Just below the head, a hole runs through the shaft. Specks of red near the point may be pigment or corrosion. The object is 18.2 cm (7⅛ in.) high and was made by Moche metalworkers on the north coast of Peru.

heading: A Distant View of Yokohama Honmura, the Licensed District, Noge Bridge, and Yoshida Bridge, from the Entrance to Yokohama near the Mountain Pass at Noge Village. Japan, Edo period, 3rd month, 1860. Utagawa (Gountei) Sadahide (Japanese, 1807–1873). Woodblock print; ink and color on paper.
paragraph: Framed by the steep walls of the cutting at Noge and by leaning pines, a small party of travelers pauses above the new port of Yokohama. Two men walk ahead. One wears a green jacket with a white crest and the other carries a bundle on his back. Two women follow below, and a fan lies at the lower left. Beyond the bridges and the licensed quarter, square-rigged foreign ships crowd the bay. Yokohama had opened to foreign trade only the year before, in 1859, and Sadahide pictured it many times for buyers eager to see it. The signature at lower right reads Gountei Sadahide.

heading: Cuirassier. France, 1872. Edouard Detaille (French, Paris 1848–1912 Paris). Watercolor on paper.
paragraph: A cuirassier, one of the heavy cavalrymen of the French army, stands at ease in full dress. His gloved hand rests on his sword hilt and his black horse waits behind him. Detaille painted the helmet with its red plume and horsehair mane, the gold aiguillettes, the red sash and the tall boots with the near-documentary care that made his name as a painter of soldiers. He signed and dated the sheet at lower left. It is small, under 26 centimeters high, yet the figure has a portrait's presence. Only a cast shadow interrupts the bare brown ground, which keeps attention on the uniform.

heading: Worker Shabti of Henettawy (C), Daughter of Isetemkheb. Egypt, Thebes, Deir el-Bahri, Tomb MMA 60. Third Intermediate Period, Dynasty 21, about 990–970 B.C. Faience.
paragraph: Shabtis were placed in Egyptian tombs to do, in the deceased's place, any labor demanded of them in the afterlife. This "worker" figure, under 12 centimeters tall, was made for a woman named Henettawy, daughter of Isetemkheb. It comes from a family tomb at Deir el-Bahri in western Thebes. It has the mummiform shape: a wrapped body with feet on a low base, arms crossed on the chest, and a long wig falling over the shoulders. The bright turquoise glaze has worn through in pale patches, and dark traces near the hands may be remains of painted hoes. Burials of this period often held hundreds of such figures.

heading: Edward I, from the English Monarchs series. Geneva, 1731–32. Jean Dassier (Geneva 1676–1763 Geneva). Bronze.
paragraph: The legend around this crowned bust reads, in part, EDOUARD I D G ANG ET HIB REX, which means "Edward I, by the grace of God, King of England and Ireland." The portrait is not a true likeness. Edward died in 1307, and this idealized face, with long curled hair, a jeweled crown and a mantle fastened with a jeweled clasp, is an eighteenth-century invention. The medal belongs to the Geneva medalist Jean Dassier's series of English monarchs, which was sold as sets to collectors. It is only 41 millimeters across. The photograph shows the obverse only. In this series the reverse carries a historical inscription.

heading: Fragment of a kylix (drinking cup), Greek, Attic, Late Archaic, 490–480 BCE; terracotta
paragraph: This sherd, about 2 cm long, was broken from an Athenian kylix, a shallow two-handled cup used for wine. The orange areas are bare clay. The dark areas were painted in a glossy black slip that turned black in firing. The tongue-shaped reserved areas set against the black suggest the red-figure technique. Red-figure was then the leading style in Athenian workshops, during the generation of the great cup painters. The fragment is too small to show what the scene was or who painted it. It was given to the Museum in 2011 by Dietrich von Bothmer, a curator who built a large study collection of such fragments.

heading: Twelve-pointed star tile, attributed to Khargird, Iran, dated 846 AH/1442–43 CE; stonepaste, polychrome glaze within black wax-resist outlines (cuerda seca)
paragraph: This tile, about 40 cm across, is dated to the reign of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh. It is attributed to Khargird in eastern Iran, where a madrasa was completed for him in these years. Tiles like it were set into walls together with complementary shapes. Its design has six-fold symmetry. White strapwork forms pointed lobed medallions on a cobalt-blue ground, and in each one sits a red-and-yellow blossom around a central rosette. A turquoise band runs along the edge. The black wax-resist lines kept the coloured glazes apart during firing, the cuerda seca technique. The glaze is crazed, and the body shows at the chipped points.

heading: Bottom of a vessel with foot, Coptic, made in Kharga Oasis, Byzantine Egypt, 4th–early 5th century; glass
paragraph: This tiny fragment, only 2.3 cm across, is the base of a small glass vessel. The dark glass rises into a pushed-in dome at the centre. Around it, an opaque white trail was laid on while the glass was hot, forming a ring foot for the vessel to stand on. Soil is still caught in its hollows. The piece was made in the Kharga Oasis in Egypt's Western Desert. It was acquired in 1908, the year the Museum began excavating there. Small, everyday glass vessels with contrasting applied trails were common in late Roman and early Byzantine Egypt.

heading: Rattle, probably Bribri, Talamanca, Costa Rica, ca. 1873; gourd, bone, cord
paragraph: This shaken rattle is 18.5 cm long and weighs only 41 grams. Its head is a dried gourd, and the seeds or pebbles inside sound when it is moved. Cord threaded through a row of holes pierced around the gourd's narrow end binds the head tightly to a bone handle, which still has its joint at the end. The rattle was probably made by a Bribri maker in the Talamanca region of southern Costa Rica. Among the Bribri, rattles are associated with the chants of ritual healers. It came to the Museum in 1889 with the Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments.

heading: Side chair, Gothic Revival style. United States, 1850–60. Maker unidentified. Wood, with silk damask upholstery and brass casters.
paragraph: The chair applies the architecture of a Gothic church to a piece of furniture. Its upholstered back rises to a pointed arch that stands more than four feet tall. The arch carries carved crockets and ends in a fleur-de-lis finial. Ring-turned posts, cut like stalks of bamboo, stand at either side and end in slender pinnacles. Pieces like this were made for the Gothic villas and libraries that were fashionable in mid-century America, and they were meant to look picturesque more than to be practical. The red damask, a pattern of lozenges and medallions, is probably a later replacement. The casters let the heavy chair be moved across the room.

paragraph: Travelers climb the steep cutting through the hill at Noge. Two men walk ahead, and behind them come women and children. Between the cliff walls, which are framed by pines, the view opens onto Yokohama: the town, its licensed district and its bridges, with a harbor full of ships beyond. The port had been opened to foreign trade only the year before, in 1859, and Sadahide became one of the most prolific artists to record it. Prints like this one sold to a public curious about the new port. A red cartouche at the top holds a descriptive inscription. The red cartouche at lower right holds the artist's signature, and seals sit beside it.

Fragments like this one are studied because they keep the painter's brushwork and the quality of the gloss.

heading: Cylinder seal with animals, serpent and tree, shown with a modern impression. Cyprus, Late Cypriot period, ca. 15th–13th century B.C. Carver unknown. Steatite.
paragraph: A cylinder seal was rolled across wet clay to leave its owner's mark, and it was usually pierced lengthwise so that it could be worn on a cord. This seal is just over 3 centimeters tall. The impression beside it shows the full design. Horned animals, probably goats or gazelles, stand in a row. Among them are a rearing serpent, a long-necked bird, a branching tree and small star-shaped motifs. The figures are cut in the soft stone with simple drilled and linear strokes. Cypriot carvers took both the seal form and its animal imagery from the Near East and adapted them in their own way.

heading: Cuirassier. France, 1872. Edouard Detaille (French, Paris 1848–1912 Paris). Watercolor on paper
paragraph: Detaille was twenty-four when he painted this cavalryman, and he would go on to become France's leading painter of military life. The trooper has dismounted and stands at ease beside a dark horse, one gloved hand resting on his sword. He wears a brass helmet with a red plume and a long horsehair mane, a blue coat with red facings, a red sash, white breeches and tall jackboots. There is no setting, only a plain brown ground, so every piece of equipment reads clearly. The sheet is signed lower left and dated 1872, the year after the Franco-Prussian War, in which Detaille served.

heading: Twelve-Pointed Star-Shaped Tile. Iran, attributed to Khargird, dated 846 AH/1442–43 CE. Stonepaste; polychrome glaze within black wax resist outlines (cuerda seca technique)
paragraph: This star tile is dated 846 AH (1442–43 CE). It is attributed to Khargird in northeastern Iran, where the Ghiyathiyya madrasa was being completed in those years for a vizier of the Timurid ruler Shah Rukh. A white strapwork rosette lies over a cobalt ground framed in turquoise, with red-brown and yellow blossoms and white buds in its twelve points. Each colour was fired in its own field, kept apart by lines of wax resist. This is the cuerda seca ("dry cord") technique. The tile, about 40 cm across, would have been set into a wall among other tiles. The glaze is crazed and the edges are chipped.

heading: Couteau de Brèche (staff weapon). France, ca. 1500. Steel, wood (beech)
paragraph: A couteau de brèche is a staff weapon with a long, knife-like blade mounted on a pole. Infantry carried it in France around 1500, and guards carried it later. This example has a slender steel head 61 cm long. One edge of the blade steps in sharply about a third of the way up, and from there the head narrows to a long, sharp point for thrusting. A faceted socket fixes the head to a beech shaft, of which only the top shows here. The complete weapon is nearly two metres long, so it could cut and thrust from well beyond the reach of a sword.

heading: Worker Shabti of Henettawy (C), Daughter of Isetemkheb. Egypt, Thebes, Deir el-Bahri, Tomb MMA 60; Third Intermediate Period, Dynasty 21, ca. 990–970 BCE. Faience
paragraph: This worker shabti, 11.9 cm high, was made for Henettawy (C), daughter of Isetemkheb. It dates to Dynasty 21, about 990–970 BCE, and comes from Tomb MMA 60 at Deir el-Bahri in Thebes, where she was buried. The figure is mummiform, with arms crossed over the chest and a long tripartite wig. The bright turquoise-blue faience is typical of the period and is now spotted with dark patches. At this time a single burial could hold hundreds of such figures, ready to stand in for the dead when work was demanded in the fields of the afterlife. No tools or inscription can be seen from this side.

heading: Bottom of a vessel with foot. Egypt, Kharga Oasis, 4th–early 5th century. Glass
paragraph: This fragment is only 2.3 centimetres across. It is the bottom of a small glass vessel, seen from below. The white ring is the vessel's foot, a thread of opaque white glass applied to the very dark, almost black body while both were hot. The hollow inside the ring is the underside of the vessel itself. Everything above it has broken away. The vessel was made in the Kharga Oasis, in Egypt's Western Desert, during the 4th or early 5th century, when Egypt was under Roman rule. A pale, gritty deposit, probably soil, still clings inside the foot. The fragment entered the museum in 1908.

heading: Pin with animal. Moche, Peru, 2nd–7th century. Cast copper
paragraph: This pin is 18.2 centimetres long. A Moche metalworker cast it in copper on the north coast of Peru. Its openwork head shows an animal, perhaps more than one, but the details are worn and hard to read. A small hole pierces the shaft just below the head, and a cord may once have passed through it. The museum's record gives the title "Pin with Animal" but lists the object type as "knife." The round, pointed shaft shows no cutting edge, so we describe it here as a pin. A touch of red remains on the lower shaft.

heading: Edward I, from the English Monarchs series. Jean Dassier (Geneva 1676–1763 Geneva), 1731–32. Bronze
paragraph: Edward I ruled England from 1272 to 1307. He is shown here as a crowned, draped bust, with wavy hair falling to his shoulders and a beaded chain clasping his cloak across his chest. The legend reads EDOUARD·I·D·G·ANG·ET·HIB·REX, "Edward I, by the grace of God, King of England and Ireland." The French spelling of his name reflects the Genevan engraver Jean Dassier. In 1731–32 Dassier issued a series of medals of English monarchs for collectors. The portrait is imagined, not taken from life. The medal is 41 millimetres across. On medals in this series the reverse usually carries a Latin summary of the reign, but it is not shown here.

heading: Rattle. Probably Bribri, Talamanca, Costa Rica, about 1873. Gourd, bone, cord
paragraph: When this rattle was shaken, whatever lies inside its hollow, egg-shaped gourd made the sound. The photograph does not show what is inside. The handle is a bone, apparently an animal long bone, with its knobbed joint end left at the base. It fits into the gourd's narrow end and is lashed in place with cord threaded through a ring of small holes pierced around the opening. The rattle is 18.5 centimetres long and weighs only 41 grams. It was made about 1873, probably by Bribri people of the Talamanca region of Costa Rica. It entered the museum in 1889 as part of the Crosby Brown Collection of Musical Instruments.
